Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

fastsae 1.0.0

fastsae 1.0.0 adds hierarchical Bayes (HB) models, the two-fold sub-area model and post-estimation tools to the frequentist EBLUP functions of 0.1.0, and corrects several estimators of 0.1.0. The changes below are relative to fastsae 0.1.0 on CRAN.

Breaking changes for users of 0.1.0

  • All EBLUP functions choose the MSE with mse_type, which includes "none" (no MSE; mse and rse are NA): eblup_fh() ("analytical", "none"), eblup_sfh() ("analytical", "pbmse", "npbmse", "none"), eblup_stfh() and eblup_twofold() ("analytical", "bootstrap", "none") and eblup_bhf() ("bootstrap", "none"). The chosen value is returned in mse_type.
    • eblup_sfh(mse_method = ) and compute_mse = of eblup_stfh() and eblup_bhf() are deprecated and still work with a warning (compute_mse = FALSE is mse_type = "none").
    • The MSE is now computed by default: eblup_stfh() gives the analytical MSE and eblup_bhf() the bootstrap MSE (both gave none before). Use mse_type = "none" for the previous output.
    • New arguments were inserted before existing ones (transform and mse_type in eblup_fh(), mse_type in eblup_sfh()), so calls that pass the later arguments by position change meaning; calls by name are unaffected.
  • eblup_bhf(): fit$lme (the lmerMod object) is replaced by fit$residuals (unit-level conditional residuals, used by residuals()), since the model is now fitted in C++ (see below); the standard errors in estcoef are (X′V̂−1X)−1(X'\hat V^{-1}X)^{-1} as in ‘lme4’.
  • goodness of eblup_fh(), eblup_sfh() and eblup_stfh() follows one convention: loglikelihood is the full Gaussian log-likelihood at the estimates, and AIC/BIC are computed from it for ML and REML fits, as in ‘sae’ and Marhuenda, Morales and Pardo (2014). In eblup_stfh() the element loglike is renamed loglikelihood.
  • Convergence problems are reported as a warning that can be caught. Before, eblup_fh(), eblup_sfh() and eblup_stfh() only printed a message and eblup_bhf() said nothing.
  • Inputs are checked before fitting, so some calls that ran before now stop with a clear message: vardir must be finite and positive in every sampled area; linearly dependent covariates stop the fit and name the aliased column (the compiled code used an approximate solution of a singular system); there must be more sampled areas than coefficients (all MSEs were NA); W of eblup_sfh() and eblup_stfh() must be non-negative (a zero row or rows that do not sum to 1 give a warning, since the SAR model with rho in (-1, 1) assumes a row-standardised W, as ‘sae’ requires); a missing population mean in eblup_bhf() names the domain. Duplicated domain values give a warning.
  • A fixed seed of eblup_sfh(), eblup_stfh() and eblup_bhf() no longer changes the random number stream of the session; the bootstrap MSEs are unchanged.
  • mys_proxmat is now the row-standardised 4-nearest-neighbour graph of the 42 areas (symmetric, 4 to 8 neighbours per area, built by data-raw/mys_proxmat.R). It was a dense distance-decay matrix with almost equal weights, which a CAR model reads as a complete graph, and its documentation wrongly said it was based on contiguous boundaries. Results that use mys_proxmat change.
  • Several estimators of 0.1.0 were corrected, which changes their results (see “Changes to the models of 0.1.0”); the most visible are the spatio-temporal model on unsorted panels such as mys_panel, its analytical and bootstrap MSE, and the spatial model with unsampled domains.

New models

Hierarchical Bayes models

  • hb_area(): area-level HB models with Gaussian, beta, binomial, Poisson, negative binomial and gamma likelihoods; iid, Besag (ICAR), BYM, BYM2, Leroux ("leroux"/"generic1"), SAR ("sar", the Bayesian counterpart of eblup_sfh()) and spatial lag ("slm") area effects; RW1, RW2, AR(1) and iid time effects; and the four space-time interactions of Knorr-Held (2000), area-specific trends and separable fields. Areas without a direct estimate are predicted. With vardir, the dispersion of each area follows from its sampling variance:
    • beta: the precision ϕd=μ̂d(1−μ̂d)/Vd−1\phi_d = \hat\mu_d(1 - \hat\mu_d)/V_d - 1 at the posterior mean of a first fit (two stages). At the direct estimate, the model variance was Vdμd(1−μd)/(yd(1−yd))V_d \mu_d(1 - \mu_d)/(y_d(1 - y_d)), not VdV_d, and the 95% intervals covered 81-84% of true proportions near 0.08, against 90-94% (benchmarks/validation/beta_vardir_phi.R);
    • negative binomial: the size n=μ̂2/(V−μ̂)n = \hat\mu^2/(V - \hat\mu) at the posterior mean of a first fit (a near-Poisson size when V≤μ̂V \le \hat\mu); the 95% intervals covered 90-95% (benchmarks/validation/dispersion_vardir.R, nb_size_prior.R);
    • gamma: the shape y2/Vy^2/V of each area.
    Without vardir, the gamma, negative binomial and Gaussian dispersions are only weakly identified with one observation per area, and hb_area() warns. inla_engine(link = ) sets the link ("probit", "cloglog" and "loglog" for binomial and beta).
  • hb_unit(): unit-level HB models (Gaussian, Bernoulli or Poisson units; iid, Besag or BYM2 domain effects), with finite population means when popsize_var is given: the non-sampled part is predicted at the non-sampled covariate mean x‾d,r=(NdX‾d−ndx‾d,s)/(Nd−nd)\bar x_{d,r} = (N_d \bar X_d - n_d \bar x_{d,s})/(N_d - n_d), and its posterior SD includes σe2/(Nd−nd)\sigma_e^2/(N_d - n_d). For binomial and Poisson units the domain means are approximate (the non-sampled part is predicted at the mean covariates; -8% and -16% bias in a simulation) and hb_unit() warns; unbiased estimation needs unit-level population covariates (Molina and Rao, 2010). The responses are checked (0/1 for binomial, non-negative integers for Poisson).
  • hb_twofold(): the two-fold sub-area model with an iid, Besag or BYM2 area effect and an iid sub-area effect (Gaussian, binomial, Poisson), with weighted area aggregates in df_area (Gaussian: exact INLA linear combinations; binomial and Poisson: draws from the Gaussian approximation of the latent field at INLA’s configurations, inla_engine(draws = 2000) by default). Missing or negative weights give a warning.
  • Estimation engines: inla_engine() (default) and jax_engine() hold all settings of an engine, so the model functions only describe the model; engine = "inla" or "jax" take the defaults. inla_engine(strategy, link, scale_model, prior_*, draws, seed, ...) passes ... to INLA::inla() and merges control.* lists with the package defaults. jax_engine() fits the same models by NumPyro NUTS on JAX (CPU, NVIDIA GPU, or the Apple GPU with device = "metal") through ‘reticulate’, with prior_beta = "horseshoe" and robust = TRUE (Student-t random effects) as options. MCMC fits report the rank-normalized split R-hat and bulk/tail ESS of every parameter (Vehtari et al., 2021; identical to ‘posterior’), divergences and tree-depth hits, warn for R-hat >= 1.05, ESS below 100 per chain and divergent transitions, and autoplot(type = "trace") / "rank" plot the chains. The engine settings are returned in engine_spec.
  • setup_numpyro_env() installs the Python side, and setup_numpyro_env(check_only = TRUE) checks it without installing or searching the system for Python (about one second).

Default priors and INLA settings of the HB models

  • The random-effect standard deviations get a half-normal prior with the scale of the response, sd(y), for Gaussian models and half-normal(1) on the link scale otherwise, instead of INLA’s PC prior P(σ>1)=0.01P(\sigma > 1) = 0.01, which depends on the unit of the response (on mys with the response in tenths it moved the estimates by up to 4.1 posterior SD). In simulations the 95% intervals covered 93-97% with the half-normal prior (EBLUP: 93-96%) and 85-95% with PC priors scaled to sd(y) (benchmarks/validation/default_sd_prior*.R).
  • The Gaussian residual SD without vardir gets the half-normal(sd y) prior (INLA’s default put it near zero, with 0-4% coverage); the negative binomial size and the gamma precision a half-normal(10) prior (INLA’s defaults put them at 110-180 and 76-84 whatever the truth); the beta precision without vardir or trials INLA’s log-gamma(1, 0.1); Leroux’s λ\lambda and the SAR/SLM ρ\rho a uniform prior. jax_engine(priors = "inla"), the default, uses the same priors, so the two engines agree within Monte Carlo error and the INLA approximation; priors = "weakly_informative" keeps the earlier NumPyro priors.
  • Gaussian models, and the Leroux and SLM effects for any family, are fitted in INLA’s "classic" mode, the other models in its "compact" mode; Gaussian models with a type I-IV interaction and three hyperparameters integrate over a grid. In comparisons with exact posteriors and long Stan runs (benchmarks/validation), the compact mode overstated the posterior SDs of Gaussian models by up to 18%, while the classic mode was within 0.07 posterior SD (means) and 0.91-1.03 times (SDs); for the other families both modes matched Stan and compact was much faster. inla_engine(inla.mode = , control.inla = ) overrides this.
  • Space-time interactions with a random walk in time carry all the constraints of Knorr-Held (2000), so domains without direct estimates are identified; the "separable" field with a random walk and the "domain-specific" RW2 stop with an error.
  • CAR models ("besag", "bym", "bym2", "leroux") use only the pattern W > 0; a dense W such as distance-decay weights gives a warning.
  • Variance components are reported as posterior means of the variance, E[1/τ∣y]E[1/\tau \mid y].
  • Posterior draws of the INLA engine are reproducible: inla_engine(seed = 1L) is the default and the seed is also set on the R side; the session’s random number stream is restored.
  • The new vignette “Default Priors of the Hierarchical Bayes Models” documents the priors of both engines and the simulations behind them.

Frequentist models and options

  • eblup_twofold(): the two-fold sub-area model of Torabi and Rao (2014) by REML or ML, with the analytical MSE g1+g2+2g3g_1 + g_2 + 2g_3 (minus the ML bias term) or a parametric bootstrap, and the area means θi=∑jwijθij\theta_i = \sum_j w_{ij}\theta_{ij} in df_area with an MSE that includes the covariances of the sub-area errors (weight, compute_area). With one sub-area per area, Fisher scoring uses the pseudo-inverse of the singular information; a negative second-order MSE is set to NA with a warning.
  • eblup_fh(transform = "log"): Fay-Herriot model on the log scale, back-transformed with the conditional-mean correction exp⁡(μ̃+g1/2)\exp(\tilde\mu + g_1/2) and a delta-method MSE (not the full Slud-Maiti second-order correction); unsampled domains get exp⁡(x′β̂+σ̂u2/2)\exp(x'\hat\beta + \hat\sigma^2_u/2).
  • Self-benchmarking (self_benchmark, benchmark_weight, benchmark_target, benchmark_group) in the EBLUP functions (augmented model of Wang, Fuller and Qu, 2008) and in hb_area() (every posterior draw is benchmarked by default, benchmark_method = "posterior", so the constraint is exact and the intervals refer to the benchmarked estimator; "wfq" uses the augmented model). With transform = "log", eblup_fh() ratio-benchmarks on the original scale.

New post-estimation tools and utilities

  • benchmark_sae(): ratio, difference, MSE-weighted (“optimal”) and logit benchmarking to one or two levels of targets (Datta et al., 2011; Bell, Datta and Ghosh, 2013; two-stage benchmarking in the spirit of Ghosh and Steorts, 2013). The optimal adjustment is proportional to wiMSEiw_i\,\mathrm{MSE}_i and uses the full MSE matrix of FH, SFH, STFH and area-level HB fits; mse_benchmarked is a first-order MSE of the benchmarked estimates. Missing or non-finite targets and missing weights stop with an error.
  • diagnose(): the goodness-of-fit statistic of Brown et al. (2001) with an upper-tail χ2\chi^2 decision (as emdi::compare.fh), a descriptive bias regression, standardised residuals (y−θ̂)/vardir−MSE(y - \hat\theta)/\sqrt{vardir - MSE}, Moran’s I of the residuals, DIC, WAIC and CPO/PIT for HB fits, and simulation metrics when the truth is known.
  • compare_sae(): agreement of two models by the mean difference and 95% limits of agreement (Bland and Altman, 1986), Lin’s (1989) concordance correlation, differences relative to the RMSE, rank changes and the overlap of the highest and lowest domains (top). Pearson’s correlation is not reported, since it measures association, not agreement. Between an HB and an EBLUP fit it reports which has the lower reported uncertainty and notes that a posterior variance and an MSE are not the same quantity. autoplot(type = "difference") is a Bland-Altman plot.
  • step_sae(): stepwise covariate selection for every model, refitting with the same settings: AIC, BIC (default) or KIC from the full log-likelihood for EBLUP models (Marhuenda, Morales and Pardo, 2014; models with a method are searched by ML and refitted with the original method; on mys the path equals emdi::step()), and LCPO, WAIC or DIC for HB models (benchmarks/validation/step_sae.R).
  • add_reliability_flags(), export_sae(), map_sae(): reliability tiers by RSE (default cut-offs of BPS-Statistics Indonesia: RSE <= 25% reliable, 25-50% use with caution, > 50% unreliable), export of estimates and model summaries to Excel or CSV, and choropleth maps of estimates, RSE, reliability, differences and benchmarking (any sf geometry column).
  • create_weights() builds spatial weights (queen, rook, k-nearest neighbours, distance bands, inverse distance) from sf objects, coordinates or neighbour lists, computing distances in blocks of rows (peak memory at 10,000 domains about the size of the returned matrix); spatial_test() gives Moran’s I, LM-error and LM-lag tests (as ‘spdep’) and a recommendation from a single test at level alpha (likelihood ratio test of FH against spatial FH, both fitted by ML, when vardir is given); gvf_smooth() smooths sampling variances by a generalized variance function.
  • sim_area_data() and sim_series_data() simulate area-level and panel data for all six families with spatial (and AR(1)) effects, returning the spatial weights; the random number stream of the session is restored after seed. New datasets sim_area and sim_panel.
  • eblup_bhf() returns goodness (full log-likelihood, AIC and BIC); with method = "ML" they equal those of lme4::lmer(REML = FALSE).
  • print()/summary() show the estimation method and engine, and autoplot() labels panel and sub-area rows uniquely.

Changes to the models of 0.1.0

eblup_stfh()

  • The panel is sorted internally into the domain-major order the model requires and results are returned in the caller’s row order. Before, unsorted input was silently mis-specified, including the time-major mys_panel of the examples (where sae::eblupSTFH(), which assumes domain-major data, gives the same wrong fit).
  • Unsampled domains and missing periods: cells whose response is NA stay in the data and are predicted. The model is defined on the full domain x time grid, the variance components are estimated by REML from the sampled cells, and every cell gets the best linear unbiased predictor given the sampled data (Saei and Chambers, 2005; Benedetti et al., 2024), with the analytical MSE g1+g2+g3g_1 + g_2 + g_3 for the predicted cells and a parametric bootstrap that covers every cell. df_eblup gains a sampled column; W must include the unsampled domains. Results on complete panels are unchanged.
  • Analytical MSE: g3g_3 used the wrong matrix orientation (wrong whenever vardir is heterogeneous); it now uses the exact derivative of the EBLUP and the REML information at the final estimates, and the second-derivative term g4g_4 is included: mse = g1 + g2 + 2 g3 - g4 (relative bias -1.7% in a simulation; +2.4% without g4g_4).
  • Bootstrap MSE: the variance components are re-estimated in every replicate (they were held fixed, so g3g_3 was missed), the SAR effects are generated with the lower Cholesky factor, and non-converged replicates are replaced.
  • When the classical Fisher scoring fails or converges to a negative variance, the fit switches to constrained REML (convergence in a simulation went from 63% to 99%; interior fits are identical to sae::eblupSTFH()); convergence = FALSE is reported when the fit ends at invalid variance components. Correlations on the boundary are treated as fixed in the MSE.
  • The model is fitted by REML only, as in Marhuenda, Molina and Morales (2013); tvalue is a z-statistic.

eblup_sfh()

  • With unsampled domains, the SAR process is defined on all domains of W, so the sampled domains are fitted with the marginal covariance (before: the SAR built from W[s, s]), consistent with the kriging of the unsampled domains and with the bootstrap. Their analytical MSE includes g3g_3 (exact derivative of the kriging predictor) and the second-order bias of the plug-in g1g_1 (relative bias -3.8%, was -7.5%).
  • When the classical Fisher scoring fails or ends with σ̂2<0\hat\sigma^2 < 0, the (RE)ML likelihood is maximised under the constraints, also inside the bootstrap. A boundary ρ̂=0.999\hat\rho = 0.999 is no longer mapped to 1, and −0.999-0.999 is reported as −1-1 only when I+WI + W is non-singular.
  • A correlation on the boundary (|ρ̂|≥0.999|\hat\rho| \ge 0.999) is treated as fixed in the analytical MSE, where the Prasad-Rao expansion is not valid; for ML fits, g3g_3 and the bias term use the ML information (the REML information made the MSE explode for σ̂2≈0\hat\sigma^2 \approx 0 and ρ̂≈1\hat\rho \approx 1). These are the only cases where the MSE differs from sae::mseSFH().
  • Bootstrap replicates are no longer rejected when estimates exceed 1e6, and npbmse no longer fails when σ̂u2=0\hat\sigma^2_u = 0.

eblup_fh() and eblup_sfh()

  • A random effect variance estimated as 0 (truncated, as in ‘sae’) is reported with a message: the EBLUPs are then synthetic estimates and the MSE estimates can understate their error (Li and Lahiri, 2010).

eblup_bhf()

  • The REML/ML fit and the bootstrap MSE run in C++, with the likelihood profiled to γ=σu2/σe2≥0\gamma = \sigma_u^2/\sigma_e^2 \ge 0 and evaluated from within-domain cross-products, so σu2=0\sigma_u^2 = 0 is handled exactly. Estimates agree with ‘lme4’ and ‘sae’ up to their optimiser tolerance; the bootstrap uses the same random draws as before, n_threads runs replicates in parallel (results do not depend on it), and it uses the same population means (popnmean_xpop) as the estimate. Rank-deficient designs give an explicit error.

Performance

  • eblup_sfh() (fit, analytical MSE, kriging and the bootstrap refits) forms no D×DD \times D inverse: all terms follow from sparse Cholesky solves with (I−ρW′)(I−ρW)(I - \rho W')(I - \rho W) and M=A+σ2E′Ψ−1EM = A + \sigma^2 E'\Psi^{-1}E (RcppEigen added to LinkingTo). Analytical MSE: D=1600D = 1600 80 s -> 2.5 s; results unchanged (relative differences below 2e-10).
  • eblup_stfh() computes the REML scores, the Fisher information and the analytical MSE from the block structure of VV, without M×MM \times M matrices (M=DTM = DT): mys_panel 7.7 s -> 0.4 s; T=5T = 5, D=500D = 500 about 4 min -> 10 s; results unchanged.
  • eblup_bhf() bootstrap: cornsoybean with B=200B = 200 0.64 s -> 0.005 s.

Documentation

  • New vignettes on the HB area-level models, default priors, unit-level and two-fold models, model diagnostics, the hb_area() engines, finite population validation and benchmarks; every exported function and S3 method has examples.
  • The website moved to https://ridsonap.is-a.dev/fastsae/.

fastsae 0.1.0

CRAN release: 2026-09-30

  • Initial CRAN release.
  • High-performance area-level Fay-Herriot (FH), spatial FH (SFH) and spatio-temporal FH (STFH) models.
  • Unit-level Battese-Harter-Fuller (BHF) models via Henderson III and REML.
